title: Sleep and food
hook: he wrote frankly about his habits of eating and sleeping (Essays 3.13)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the art of conversation: Montaigne liked his talk sharp and had no use for flattery. Your line was honest talk. Did one honest conversation happen? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-two.

A philosopher at dinner bites his own tongue. Sometimes his fingers. He eats too fast, he admits, and this is what happens. Then he goes on: he loves sauces, though his father hated them. He doesn't care much for salads or fruit, except melons. He can manage dinner without a tablecloth, but a clean napkin he really wants. This isn't gossip from a servant. It's Montaigne, writing about himself, in the closing essay of his book, Of experience. Why would a serious writer put his napkins next to his thoughts on death and God? Today, sleep and food.
screen: `HE BITES HIS OWN TONGUE.` → `SAUCES, MELONS, A CLEAN NAPKIN.` → `WHY PUT THIS IN A BOOK?`

segments.voice: Start with the plain facts, because he gives them plainly. Sleep, he says, has taken up a large part of his life. He likes his bed hard, and he likes to sleep alone, well covered. He eats greedily and in a hurry. He knows which foods agree with him and which habits he'd be better off breaking. He isn't confessing. He's reporting, the way you'd describe the weather. Now the reason. Nature, Montaigne says, has been like a mother here. The things we have to do to stay alive, she made pleasant too, and she calls us to them not only through reason but through appetite. Eating and sleeping aren't a tax we pay before the real life starts. They're part of the gift. Then his quarrel, and it has an edge. Some people count an act as less worthy because it's necessary, as if eating and sleeping were beneath a serious mind. Montaigne won't have it. Nobody, he says, will get it out of his head that pleasure and necessity make a very fitting marriage. He wants the mind to keep the body company at the table, not sit apart from it, sniffing. Last, what this looks like on an ordinary day. A warm bowl of something when you're cold. The first sip of water when you're thirsty. Lying down at night and feeling the weight leave your feet. Montaigne would count every one. Not as the reward for a day well spent, but as the day itself, being lived. A man who wrote down so many doubts still thought a good night's sleep belonged in the book.
screen: `A HARD BED, A HURRIED MEAL.` · `NATURE MADE NEEDS PLEASANT.` · `PLEASURE MARRIED TO NEED.` · `THE BOWL, THE WATER, THE BED.` · then, large: `ORDINARY PLEASURES ARE PART OF THE GIFT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: enjoy one ordinary pleasure, on purpose. If there's a drink nearby, take a slow sip and actually taste it. If not, notice the pleasure that's already here: the chair holding you up, warm hands, a full breath going all the way down. Pick one. Stay with it. When your mind wanders off to the list, bring it back to the sip, the chair, the breath. No need to make it deep. Just let it be pleasant. The bell holds the time.
Sleep and food. Montaigne's frank account of his own eating and sleeping, and his claim that nature made our needs pleasant on purpose. Today's word.
Your line: ordinary pleasures. At your next meal, eat the first few bites slowly enough to notice them. Tonight, notice the moment you lie down. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-two.

screen: `DAY 1182 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT TO KEEP FROM MONTAIGNE.`

howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often take the eating and sleeping passages of Of experience as permission to treat daily needs as part of a good life rather than a distraction from it; some use them as a cue to eat one meal a day without hurry.

fork.setup: you're Montaigne, writing a serious book about how to live. do you include how you eat and sleep?
options: yes, plainly, because it's part of living.
fork.reveal: he puts them right in the closing essay, next to his thoughts on experience, because he thinks nature made our needs pleasant on purpose.

trapdoor: what you thought: sleep and food is small talk.
what it means: Montaigne says nature made our needs pleasant, and that pleasure and necessity belong together.
what a scholar hears: it comes in Of experience, the closing essay, where his habits of body sit beside his last word on how to live.

notes: Montaigne is paraphrased throughout; Cotton (1685) and Florio (1603) are public domain but not on the validator's translation list, so nothing is quoted.

Check each habit against 3.13: biting tongue and fingers from eating greedily; loving sauces his father hated; not much for salads or fruits except melons; managing without a tablecloth but not without a clean napkin; sleep taking a large part of his life; a hard bed, alone, well covered. Montaigne also gives a number of hours he sleeps; deliberately left out under the claims rule.
'Instead of turning into angels, they turn into beasts' paraphrases a well-known line of 3.13; day 1171 or 1173 may already use it. Cut here if it repeats.
'He spent years writing down his doubts' is a general description drawn from earlier days of the block; cut if the claims editor prefers.
